passages.text: As someone who has taught in state schools for twenty-three years, I have watched successive governments promise to fix school funding and then quietly abandon those promises the moment the cameras turn elsewhere. I have seen classrooms where textbooks are shared between three students. I have covered lessons in corridors because there were not enough rooms. Last year I was named Regional Teacher of the Year, and I can tell you with absolute certainty that the award meant less to me than the knowledge that twelve of my students could not afford the revision guides they needed for their exams. I am not a politician. I am not campaigning for a headline. I am a teacher who has spent over two decades watching this crisis deepen, and I am asking you to listen not because I am dramatic, but because I have earned the right to be heard.
passages.label: Model A — Ethos: Authority and Credibility

passages.text: The numbers do not lie. In 2024, the average secondary school in England lost £350,000 in real-terms funding compared to 2010. That is not an opinion — it is a figure published by the Institute for Fiscal Studies. Consider what that money represents: fourteen teaching assistants, or an entire science department’s annual budget for equipment, or three years of heating bills. Schools cannot choose which of these to sacrifice without students suffering. Meanwhile, a recent survey of 2,000 parents found that 68% had been asked to contribute towards basic classroom resources. The logical conclusion is unavoidable. If funding continues to fall at the current rate, one in five schools will be unable to deliver the full curriculum by 2028. This is not alarmism. It is arithmetic.
passages.label: Model B — Logos: Logic and Evidence

passages.text: Imagine a fourteen-year-old girl sitting in a maths lesson. She is bright, curious, and desperate to do well. But the classroom is freezing because the heating has been broken since October and nobody has the budget to fix it. She is wearing her coat over her blazer, and her fingers are so cold she keeps dropping her pen. She has not eaten breakfast because there is nothing in the cupboard at home, and the free school meal she relies on is still two hours away. She will not ask for help because she has learned that drawing attention to yourself in a class of thirty-four is a risk she cannot afford. This girl is not a statistic. She is in your community, in your town, walking past your house every morning. And she is being failed — not by her own lack of effort, but by a system that has decided she is not worth the investment.
passages.label: Model C — Pathos: Emotion and Empathy

passages.text: I have coached grassroots football for fifteen years, working with over six hundred young players across our borough. In that time I have watched three local pitches close, two clubhouses demolished, and council funding for junior sport cut by 41%. Those are the facts, and they should alarm every one of you. But what the figures cannot capture is the boy who turned up last Tuesday evening with holes in his trainers and told me that football practice was the only hour of the week he felt safe. Or the girl who said she wanted to be a physiotherapist and asked if I could help her study anatomy — because there was no one at home who could. These young people are not asking for luxuries. They are asking for a pitch, a coach, and two hours away from streets that offer them nothing. If we — as a community — cannot provide that, then we have forfeited the right to complain when things go wrong.
passages.label: Model D — Blended: All Three Modes Combined

passages.text: School funding is a problem. There isn’t enough money and this means that schools can’t buy all the stuff they need. Some schools don’t have enough textbooks and some schools have old computers. I think the government should give more money to schools because education is important. If they don’t then things will get worse and that would be bad. Teachers work really hard and they deserve better. Students also deserve better because they are the future. It’s not fair that some schools have more money than others. I think everyone would agree that this needs to change. Something should be done about it and it should be done soon.
passages.label: Weak Version — No Rhetorical Strategy

method_card.title: The Three Pillars of Persuasion
method_card.content: Every persuasive text relies on three modes: ethos (credibility — why should they trust you?), logos (logic — what's the evidence?), and pathos (emotion — how do you make them feel?). The strongest writing blends all three, but knowing which to lead with depends on your audience and purpose.

exam_context.frequency: Every Paper 2 includes a transactional writing task — understanding persuasion underpins every response

gold.context: A good response uses ethos (establishes the speaker's credibility or personal connection), logos (includes at least one statistic, fact, or piece of logical reasoning), and pathos (creates an emotional image or appeal using a specific person or moment). Each mode should be clearly identifiable and purposeful, not just vaguely present. The writing should feel like a real speech with direct address and a confident tone.
gold.question: A local youth centre is under threat of closure due to council budget cuts. Write the opening of a speech to a council meeting arguing that the centre must be saved. Use ALL THREE modes of persuasion (ethos, logos, pathos) deliberately and effectively.

gold.context: A good response leads with evidence and reasoning rather than emotion. It includes at least two specific facts, statistics, or logical claims that build on each other. The argument should feel like it would convince a sceptical reader through the strength of its evidence, not just the force of its feeling.
gold.question: Write a paragraph for a newspaper article arguing that schools should receive more funding. Use logos as your DOMINANT mode of persuasion — build your argument primarily through statistics, logical reasoning, and evidence. You may include brief ethos or pathos, but logic must drive the argument.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.content: Consider what the writer is doing in this opening. They are telling us about their personal experience — twenty-three years of teaching — before making any argument. This is not emotion and it is not statistics. It is credibility.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.content: Name the mode. When a writer establishes why they should be trusted — through experience, expertise, or moral authority — that is ethos. Here, the length of service ('twenty-three years') is the writer's qualification.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.content: Notice how the ethos is woven into the argument rather than stated bluntly. The writer does not say 'I am an expert.' Instead, the experience is shown through specific detail — watching governments 'promise to fix school funding and then quietly abandon those promises.' The word 'quietly' implies the writer has been paying close attention.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: The writer uses ethos to build credibility. By referencing twenty-three years of teaching experience, they position themselves as someone who has earned the right to comment on school funding. The specific detail — watching promises be 'quietly' abandoned — shows sustained, first-hand observation rather than casual opinion, making the reader more likely to trust what follows.

worked_examples.question: Which mode of persuasion is the writer using here, and how does it work?

steps.label: Step 1
steps.content: In this example, the writer begins with ethos — 'fifteen years' of coaching and 'six hundred young players.' This establishes personal authority before any argument is made.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.content: Notice the shift to logos. The writer provides specific, verifiable data: 'three local pitches close, two clubhouses demolished, and council funding for junior sport cut by 41%.' The precision of '41%' makes the decline feel measured and factual rather than exaggerated.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.content: Now consider the pivot — 'But what the figures cannot capture.' This single sentence transitions the reader from logos to pathos. The writer acknowledges the power of statistics and then deliberately moves beyond them, signalling that something more important is coming.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.content: The pathos arrives with the anecdote about the boy with 'holes in his trainers' who said football practice was 'the only hour of the week he felt safe.' This is a specific, individual story — it puts a human face on the statistics and appeals directly to the reader's empathy.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: The writer blends all three modes of persuasion. Ethos establishes authority (fifteen years of coaching), logos provides hard evidence (the 41% funding cut and specific closures), and pathos delivers an emotional punch through the anecdote of the boy who felt safe only at football practice. The pivot — 'what the figures cannot capture' — is particularly effective because it tells the reader that the facts alone are not enough, preparing them to respond emotionally. By layering all three modes, the writer leaves the audience with both rational and emotional reasons to act.

ai_marking_prompts.creative_writing:
You are a GCSE English Language tutor giving formative feedback on a student's short creative writing (around 80-120 words). This is a practice task — your goal is to encourage and develop.

Assess whether the student:
1. Created a clear ATMOSPHERE or MOOD through their writing choices
2. Used SPECIFIC detail rather than vague generalisations
3. Showed some CRAFT — deliberate vocabulary choices, varied sentences, or figurative language
4. Engaged the reader — does the writing create a picture or feeling?

IMPORTANT: This is short creative writing, not an essay. Reward imagination and voice. A student who writes vividly about a simple scene is doing better than one who uses forced figurative language on every line. Quality over quantity. Be genuinely encouraging — creative writing is personal and students need confidence.

{"quality":"excellent|good|needs_work|not_valid","feedback":"2-3 sentences","improvement":"optional suggestion"}

excellent = vivid, engaging writing with clear atmosphere, specific detail, and deliberate craft. Shows a genuine writer's voice

Assess whether the student:

2. Used a range of TECHNIQUES — sensory language, figurative language, varied sentence structures, effective punctuation

passages.text: We are the generation that inherited a warming planet, that watched the glaciers retreat, that read the headlines and hoped somebody else would act. We are the generation that was told recycling would save us, that carbon targets were being met, that technology would find a way. We are the generation that now knows all of that was a lie. The ice caps do not care about your optimism. The rising seas do not negotiate. The wildfires burning across three continents right now will not pause while we hold another summit and draft another pledge. We need action, not applause. We need legislation, not likes. We need sacrifice, not slogans. Because the alternative — the world we hand to our children if we do nothing — is not a world at all. It is a warning we chose to ignore.
passages.label: Model A — Powerful Rhetorical Devices (Speech on Climate)

passages.text: A smartphone is a library, a calculator, and a camera. It is also a distraction, a weapon, and a thief of concentration. This is the paradox that every school in the country must now confront. Supporters of phone bans argue that classrooms are calmer without them, that students talk to each other more, that grades improve. They are right. But opponents argue that banning phones teaches young people nothing about self-regulation, that it treats teenagers like toddlers, that it confiscates a tool they will need every day of their adult lives. They are also right. The question, then, is not whether phones are good or bad. It is whether we trust young people enough to learn how to manage them — or whether we have already decided that they cannot.
passages.label: Model B — Powerful Rhetorical Devices (Article on School Phones)

passages.text: We need to save the planet, save our futures, and save our souls. We need to fight for justice, fight for fairness, and fight for freedom. We need to stand up, speak up, and rise up. Every day, every hour, every minute, we are destroying the world, destroying our hopes, and destroying our dreams. The oceans are dying, the forests are dying, and our ambitions are dying. How long will we wait? How long will we watch? How long will we wonder? It is time to act, time to change, and time to believe. The world needs heroes, the world needs leaders, and the world needs us. We must be brave, be bold, and be brilliant.
passages.label: Weak Version A — Overdone Devices (Forced Tricolon)

passages.text: Don’t you think school uniforms are bad? Wouldn’t you agree that they cost too much? Isn’t it true that nobody actually likes wearing them? Who decided that a blazer makes you learn better? What is the point of a tie, really? Can anyone honestly say that wearing grey trousers has ever improved anyone’s grade? The answer, obviously, is no. No, no, and no again. School uniforms are, without any shadow of a doubt whatsoever, the single worst invention in the entire history of education. They crush individuality like a boot crushes an ant. They destroy self-expression like a wrecking ball destroys a building. Something must be done, and that something is abolishing uniforms forever.
passages.label: Weak Version B — Clumsy Devices (Awkward Rhetorical Questions)

passages.text: Good morning, everyone. I want to talk about something that affects every single person in this room: the food we are served at lunch. Not because I want to complain — though I could — but because I believe we deserve better, and I believe we can make it happen. Last term, a petition signed by three hundred students asked for healthier options. What changed? Nothing. The same beige trays, the same lukewarm chips, the same soggy vegetables that nobody touches. But here is what I am not asking for: I am not asking for a five-star restaurant. I am not asking for avocado toast and artisan bread. I am asking for food that tastes like food. Food that fuels us for an afternoon of learning rather than sending us into a carbohydrate coma by period five. That is not unreasonable. That is not entitled. That is common sense.
passages.label: Model C — Balanced Speech with Effective Devices

method_card.title: Rhetorical Devices That Work
method_card.content: Rhetorical devices turn ordinary sentences into memorable, persuasive ones. The key devices are: tricolon (rule of three), rhetorical questions, direct address, anaphora (deliberate repetition), antithesis (contrasting ideas), and hyperbole. Use them deliberately — one well-placed device beats five crammed into a paragraph.

prerequisites.title: Introduction to Rhetoric — Ethos, Logos, Pathos

exam_context.frequency: Rhetorical devices are expected in every Paper 2 writing response — examiners reward deliberate, effective use

gold.context: A good response uses at least three identifiable rhetorical devices (e.g. tricolon, rhetorical question, antithesis, anaphora, direct address, hyperbole) and each one serves a clear persuasive purpose. Devices should feel natural within the argument, not bolted on for effect. The speech should have a confident, engaging tone with a clear position.
gold.question: Write a short speech to your year group arguing that your school should do more to address climate change. Use at least THREE different rhetorical devices effectively — but avoid the trap of overdoing any single device. Quality matters more than quantity.

gold.context: A good response uses antithesis to dismiss an accusation of being unreasonable before stating a sensible request. The contrast should be sharp and specific — not vague. The paragraph should read naturally as part of a speech or article, with an appropriate register.
gold.question: The school canteen speech uses antithesis brilliantly ('I am not asking for a five-star restaurant... I am asking for food that tastes like food'). Write a paragraph on a different school issue where you use antithesis to pre-empt a counter-argument — show what you are NOT asking for, then what you ARE asking for.

gold.question: This passage stacks device after device with no argument in between. Take this section and rewrite it so that the tricolon is followed by a sentence of actual reasoning that explains WHY the point matters.
The phone debate article uses several subtle rhetorical techniques. Sort each one by its strategic purpose in the argument.

statements.text: "A smartphone is a library, a calculator, and a camera. It is also a distraction, a weapon, and a thief of concentration." — two contrasting tricolons
statements.explain: By giving equal weight to positives and negatives, the writer signals they are not biased — this builds credibility before the argument develops.

statements.text: "This is the paradox that every school in the country must now confront" — naming the paradox
statements.explain: Calling it a 'paradox' tells the reader there is no simple answer — this sets up the balanced, nuanced argument that follows.

statements.text: "They are right. But... They are also right." — validating both sides
statements.explain: Acknowledging both sides as valid is a sophisticated rhetorical move — it makes the reader trust the writer's judgement.

statements.text: "whether we trust young people enough" — closing question
statements.explain: The article ends by reframing the debate from phones to trust — forcing the reader to confront a deeper question about their assumptions.

statements.text: "treats teenagers like toddlers" — sharp comparison
statements.explain: This is a pathos technique — the insulting comparison provokes an emotional reaction, making the reader feel the unfairness of phone bans.

statements.text: "it confiscates a tool they will need every day of their adult lives" — forward-looking argument
statements.explain: This is logos — it makes a logical argument about the practical consequences of banning phones, looking beyond school to adult life.

gold.context: A good response makes a compelling argument against uniforms using precise, measured language. It avoids hyperbole, melodrama, and absolute claims. steps.content: Look at the structure of these three sentences. Each one follows the same pattern: 'We need [something meaningful], not [something hollow].' When a writer repeats the same opening phrase across consecutive sentences, that is anaphora.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.content: Notice that the three sentences also form a tricolon — a group of three parallel phrases. The rule of three creates a sense of rhythm and completeness, making the point feel both emphatic and finished.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.content: Consider the contrasts within each sentence. 'Action' versus 'applause,' 'legislation' versus 'likes,' 'sacrifice' versus 'slogans.' Each pair sets something genuine against something superficial. This is antithesis — placing opposing ideas side by side to sharpen the writer's argument.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: The writer combines anaphora ('We need...'), tricolon (three parallel sentences), and antithesis (contrasting genuine action with empty gestures). Together, these devices create a powerful rhythm that builds momentum and forces the reader to confront the gap between what is being done and what is needed. The repetition of 'We need' makes the demand feel urgent and non-negotiable.

steps.label: Step 2

steps.label: Step 4
steps.content: In this example, the writer knows what rhetorical questions are but does not know how to use them with restraint. The result feels aggressive rather than persuasive — the reader is lectured, not invited to think.

steps.label: Answer

passages.text: The proposal to sell Greenfield Park to a property developer should be rejected outright. This park is not an empty piece of land waiting for a purpose. It is the last remaining green space in a ward where 12,000 residents have no garden. Every weekend, families gather there. Every evening, runners circle the lake. Every morning, dog walkers meet by the bandstand and talk — the kind of ordinary, human connection that no housing estate can replace. Some will argue that the borough needs new homes, and they are right. Housing is a genuine crisis. But building on Greenfield Park does not solve it — it simply transfers one crisis into another. The developer’s plans include just 15% affordable housing, meaning the people who currently use the park could never afford to live in what replaces it. steps.label: Step 1
steps.content: Consider the very first sentence. 'The proposal to sell Greenfield Park to a property developer should be rejected outright.' The writer states their position immediately — no throat-clearing, no background. The reader knows exactly where the writer stands before the second sentence begins.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.content: Notice how the second sentence pre-empts a possible counter-argument. By saying the park 'is not an empty piece of land waiting for a purpose,' the writer dismisses the idea that selling it is a neutral or harmless act. This anticipates what the opposition might say and shuts it down early.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.content: The third sentence introduces evidence: '12,000 residents have no garden.' This is a specific figure that grounds the argument in fact, giving the emotional appeal a logical foundation. The opening moves from opinion to anticipation to evidence in just three sentences.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: The writer structures the opening in three clear moves: a bold thesis statement ('should be rejected outright'), an immediate counter to the opposition ('not an empty piece of land'), and supporting evidence ('12,000 residents have no garden'). This gives the argument instant clarity and momentum — the reader is not left guessing the writer's position, and the case begins building from the very first line.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.content: Notice the concession in the opening: 'Some will argue that the borough needs new homes, and they are right.' The writer does not dismiss the opposing view. Instead, they acknowledge it as valid — 'Housing is a genuine crisis.' This is a deliberate strategy. By agreeing with the opposition on a point of fact, the writer sounds fair and reasonable.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.content: Consider the word 'But.' This single conjunction is the turning point of the paragraph. Everything before it concedes ground; everything after it takes it back. The writer has earned the right to disagree by first showing they understand the other side.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.content: The rebuttal is precise: 'it simply transfers one crisis into another.' This reframes the proposal — instead of solving a problem, it creates a new one. The phrase is concise and memorable, which makes it harder to argue against.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.content: The final detail — 'just 15% affordable housing' — attacks the specific plan, not the general principle. The writer is saying: even if building homes were the answer, this particular development would not help the people who need it. This is logos at its sharpest.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: The writer handles the counter-argument by first conceding its validity ('they are right. Housing is a genuine crisis') and then dismantling the specific proposal rather than the principle. The pivot word 'But' shifts from agreement to rebuttal, and the phrase 'transfers one crisis into another' reframes the development as harmful rather than helpful. The statistic about 15% affordable housing provides targeted evidence that the plan would not serve the community it displaces. This concede-then-rebut structure makes the writer appear fair-minded while delivering a devastating counter-argument.

Dear Councillor Hartley,

I am writing to urge the council to install protected cycle lanes along the A452 between Kenilworth and Coventry. As a daily commuter on this road, I have witnessed three near-misses involving cyclists in the past six months alone.

The current road layout offers no safe provision for people who choose to cycle. The carriageway is narrow, the speed limit is 40mph, and drivers frequently pass within inches of riders. A protected lane — separated by a physical barrier, not merely painted lines — would transform this route from one of the most dangerous in the county to one of the safest.

I recognise that road improvements require significant investment. However, the council’s own climate action plan commits to increasing active travel by 30% before 2030. Without safe infrastructure, that target is unachievable.

I would welcome the opportunity to discuss this further and can be contacted at the address above.

Yours sincerely,
Daniel Okonkwo

passages.text:
Hey Priya,

You will never guess what happened at Glastonbury. Remember how I said I’d probably just stand at the back and eat chips? Well, I ended up right at the front for the headliner — so close I could see the drummer’s face. The bass was so loud my ribs were vibrating.

But honestly, the best bit wasn’t the music. It was the campsite at about 2am, sitting outside the tent with people we’d only met that afternoon, sharing cold pizza and talking absolute nonsense. There’s something about festivals that strips away all the awkwardness — everyone’s muddy, everyone’s tired, and nobody cares what you look like.

You should come next year. I know you said festivals aren’t your thing, but I genuinely think you’d love it. And before you mention the toilets — yes, they’re grim. But you get used to it faster than you’d think.

Miss you. Let’s catch up soon.

Ellie x

THE QUIET CRISIS NOBODY IS TALKING ABOUT
By Rashid Iqbal

One in five teenagers in Britain is currently experiencing a diagnosable mental health condition. That figure has doubled in the past decade. Yet in most schools, the entire wellbeing provision consists of a poster on a corridor wall and a suggestion box that nobody empties.

The problem is not awareness — young people know what anxiety is. The problem is access. A student referred to Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services today will wait, on average, fourteen weeks for an initial appointment. Fourteen weeks of sleepless nights, missed lessons, and silent suffering while a system that was designed to help them processes paperwork.

We do not treat broken arms this way. We do not ask a student with a fractured wrist to wait three months and then maybe see someone. Mental health deserves the same urgency, the same funding, and the same seriousness. Until it gets all three, that one-in-five statistic will only climb.
passages.label: Model C — Serious Article (Youth Mental Health)

passages.text:
THE DEFINITIVE RANKING OF SCHOOL LUNCHES (AND YES, IT’S CONTROVERSIAL)
By Jess Hargreaves

Let’s settle this once and for all. I have spent five years eating in this canteen and I have opinions. Strong ones.

At number one — and this should surprise nobody — is the Friday pizza. Crispy base, generous cheese, and the tomato sauce actually tastes like tomatoes rather than ketchup mixed with regret. It is the highlight of the week and I refuse to apologise for saying so.

At the bottom, occupying a special dungeon of disappointment, is the Wednesday pasta bake. It arrives lukewarm, leaves cold, and tastes of nothing except the faint memory of what flavour used to be. I once watched someone prod it with a fork and it didn’t move. The whole thing. Just sat there. Defiant.

Somewhere in the middle sits the jacket potato: reliable, inoffensive, and completely forgettable. The Switzerland of school meals. You won’t regret it, but you won’t remember it either.

method_card.title: Letters and Articles — Getting the Format Right
method_card.content: Letters and articles have format conventions that examiners expect. A formal letter needs addresses, a date, and appropriate sign-off. passages.text:
Good afternoon, teachers and governors. I am standing here today because a proposal has been made to cancel all residential trips for Key Stage 4 students, and I believe that proposal is a mistake we will regret for years to come.

Let me tell you about a trip I went on in Year 9. We visited the battlefields of northern France. I stood in a trench that was over a hundred years old, and I felt the mud under my shoes and the cold in my chest, and in that moment history stopped being words on a page. It became real. No textbook, no video, no classroom discussion could have given me what that experience gave me.

Trips cost money. I understand that. But so does every other investment this school makes in its students — the sports equipment, the drama studio, the new science block. Nobody questions those. What makes a residential trip different is that it teaches things no classroom can: independence, resilience, and the confidence that comes from stepping outside the world you know. Do not take that away from us.

passages.text:
Two weeks ago, I walked from my front door to the bus stop. It is a four-minute walk. In those four minutes, I counted seventeen pieces of litter on the pavement. A crushed energy drink can. A takeaway box leaking brown sauce onto the kerb. A plastic bag tangled around a lamppost like some sad, deflated flag.

Now, I could have walked past all of it. Most people do. But I want to ask you a question — and I want you to answer it honestly, even if the answer embarrasses you. When did we decide this was acceptable? When did we look at our own streets and think: yes, this is fine?

I am not asking you to become environmental activists. I am not asking you to chain yourselves to a tree. I am asking you to pick up one piece of litter a day. Just one. Because if every person in this room did that, we would remove over ten thousand pieces of rubbish from our streets every single year. That is not idealism. That is maths.
passages.label: Model B — Speech (Community Litter Campaign)

passages.text:
The argument for making Physical Education optional at GCSE level is more nuanced than it first appears. While few would dispute that exercise is beneficial for young people, the question is whether compulsory PE lessons are the most effective way to encourage lifelong physical activity — or whether they achieve the opposite.

For students who enjoy sport, PE is a highlight of the week. For those who do not, it is a source of anxiety that can damage their relationship with exercise for decades. Forcing a reluctant teenager to play rugby in the rain does not build character; it builds resentment. A more productive approach would be to offer a range of physical activities — yoga, climbing, dance, swimming — and allow students to choose.

However, removing PE entirely carries risks. Adolescent obesity rates are rising, screen time is increasing, and many students receive no physical activity outside school. The solution lies not in abolishing PE but in reforming it: making it inclusive, varied, and focused on wellbeing rather than competition.
passages.label: Model C — Essay (Should PE Be Optional at GCSE Level?)

passages.text:
In an age of infinite scrolling and six-second videos, reading a book from cover to cover has become an act of quiet rebellion. It demands patience, concentration, and the willingness to sit with someone else’s thoughts for hours at a time. These are precisely the qualities that modern life erodes, and precisely the reason reading matters more now than ever.

Research consistently shows that students who read for pleasure outperform their peers across every subject — not just English. Reading builds vocabulary, strengthens analytical thinking, and develops the kind of sustained focus that no app can replicate. It is, in effect, a form of cognitive training disguised as entertainment.

Critics may argue that young people consume more text than ever through social media and messaging. This is true, but scrolling through captions is not reading in any meaningful sense. A novel asks you to inhabit another consciousness. A tweet asks you to react. The difference between the two is the difference between thinking and performing.
passages.label: Model D — Essay (The Value of Reading for Pleasure)

SWITCHING OFF: WHY YOUR PHONE MIGHT BE THE BIGGEST BARRIER TO YOUR SUCCESS
By Naomi Chandra

Every morning, before their feet touch the floor, the average British teenager reaches for their phone. They scroll through notifications accumulated overnight, check social media feeds curated by algorithms designed to hold their attention, and absorb a stream of content that is entertaining, endless, and entirely passive. By the time they sit down in their first lesson, their concentration has already been fractured.

This is not a moral failure. It is a design feature. Technology companies employ teams of psychologists whose sole purpose is to make their products irresistible. The pull-to-refresh gesture, the infinite scroll, the red notification badge — each one is engineered to exploit the same reward pathways that make gambling addictive. To blame teenagers for succumbing to this is like blaming a fish for taking bait.

However, understanding the problem does not excuse inaction. If young people are to thrive academically and emotionally, they need strategies for managing screen time — not a lecture about willpower, but practical tools. Designated phone-free study periods, app timers, and charging stations outside the bedroom are small changes that yield significant results. The evidence is unambiguous: students who implement screen boundaries sleep better, concentrate longer, and report lower levels of anxiety. The question is not whether to act, but why we have waited so long.

By Marcus Howe

Walk through any town center in this country and you will see the same thing; pavements crammed with identicle chain stores, carparks were playgrounds used to be, and not a single tree in sight. Our towns are sufocating under concrete, and nobody seems to care.

This is not just about aesthetics. Green spaces are essential for mental health, for childrens development, and for the quality of air we breath. Without them, we are building communitys designed for cars, not people; for profit, not wellbeing; for developers, not families.

The irony is unbareable. Councils spend millions on ‘regeneration’ projects that tear down the very things that made a town worth living in. They replace parks with parking. They sacrifice playing fields for supermarkets. And then they wonder why residents feel disconected, isolated, and angry.

Its time to fight back. Its time to demand that every new development includes manditory green space. Its time to remember that a town without trees is not a town at all — its just a collection of buildings were people happen to sleep.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.content: Consider the opening image: 'before their feet touch the floor, the average British teenager reaches for their phone.' The writer begins with a specific, visual moment that most readers will recognise from their own lives. This is a hook — it grabs attention by describing something universal and immediately relatable.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.content: Notice the structure of the second sentence. It uses a tricolon: 'scroll through notifications... check social media feeds... absorb a stream of content.' The three actions build from quick (scrolling) to passive (absorbing), showing a progression from active choice to mindless consumption. The adjectives at the end — 'entertaining, endless, and entirely passive' — form their own tricolon, hammering home the point.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.content: Look at the final sentence: 'By the time they sit down in their first lesson, their concentration has already been fractured.' The word 'fractured' is a strong vocabulary choice — it suggests something broken, damaged, not just distracted. This single paragraph moves from relatable opening to specific detail to a clear thesis: phones damage concentration before school even begins.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: The writer opens with a relatable hook (the morning phone habit), builds momentum through a tricolon of increasingly passive actions ('scroll... check... absorb'), and concludes the paragraph with a thesis statement anchored by the word 'fractured' — which implies damage rather than mere distraction. This opening paragraph achieves three things in quick succession: it engages the reader, establishes the topic, and signals the writer's position. For a full response, this kind of purposeful opening sets the tone for everything that follows.

They scroll through notifications accumulated overnight, check social media feeds curated by algorithms designed to hold their attention, and absorb a stream of content that is entertaining, endless, and entirely passive. By the time they sit down in their first lesson, their concentration has already been fractured.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.content: Consider the first paragraph. It is genuinely powerful: a shocking statistic ('$1.7 trillion'), a human contrast ('35p an hour'), and a direct address that implicates the audience ('The sequinned top you bought'). This opening uses logos and pathos together and would work well in a planned response.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.content: Now notice what happens next: 'But I’m getting ahead of myself. Let me go back to the environmental side of things first. Actually, no — the human cost is more important. Or maybe they’re equally important.' The writer is thinking aloud on the page. They have not planned their structure and are making decisions about order mid-sentence.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.content: This reveals a planning failure. The writer has strong material — the statistics, the human cost, the environmental angle — but has not decided how to organise it before starting to write. In an exam, spending three to five minutes on a brief plan (thesis, three key points, counter-argument, conclusion) would prevent this kind of structural collapse.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.content: Consider how a plan would fix this. The writer could decide in advance: Paragraph 1 — hook with the human cost. Paragraph 2 — environmental damage. Paragraph 3 — counter-argument (fashion is an industry that creates jobs). Paragraph 4 — call to action. With that plan, the strong content would land in a logical sequence rather than unravelling.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: The opening paragraph is strong — it uses a shocking statistic, a human contrast, and direct address to hook the reader. However, the structure collapses immediately afterwards: 'I’m getting ahead of myself... Actually, no... Or maybe they’re equally important' reveals that the writer has not planned the order of their argument. The content is there, but without structure it feels disorganised and loses the reader's confidence. A brief plan before writing — deciding the sequence of points in advance — would allow the strong material to build logically rather than competing with itself. Planning is the difference between a response that has good ideas and one that communicates them effectively.

ai_marking_prompts.creative_writing:
You are a GCSE English Language tutor giving formative feedback on a student's short creative writing (around 80-120 words). This is a practice task — your goal is to encourage and develop.

Assess whether the student:
1. Created a clear ATMOSPHERE or MOOD through their writing choices
2. Used SPECIFIC detail rather than vague generalisations
3. Showed some CRAFT — deliberate vocabulary choices, varied sentences, or figurative language
4. Engaged the reader — does the writing create a picture or feeling?

IMPORTANT: This is short creative writing, not an essay. Reward imagination and voice. A student who writes vividly about a simple scene is doing better than one who uses forced figurative language on every line. Quality over quantity. Be genuinely encouraging — creative writing is personal and students need confidence.

Respond in JSON:
{"quality":"excellent|good|needs_work|not_valid","feedback":"2-3 sentences","improvement":"optional suggestion"}

excellent = vivid, engaging writing with clear atmosphere, specific detail, and deliberate craft. Shows a genuine writer's voice
good = creates some atmosphere or imagery, uses some specific detail, shows effort with vocabulary or technique even if inconsistent
needs_work = very generic or vague, mostly tells rather than shows, little evidence of deliberate craft
not_valid = didn't attempt creative writing, wrote a single sentence, or is completely off-topic

You are a GCSE English Language tutor giving formative feedback on a student's rewritten argument sentence. The student was shown a flat or weak argument and asked to improve it using rhetorical devices, stronger evidence, or more persuasive language.

Assess whether the student:
1. Made a genuine IMPROVEMENT in persuasive power
2. Used a rhetorical device or persuasive technique effectively (not just made it longer)

IMPORTANT: Reward any valid rhetorical improvement. If they added a rhetorical question, tricolon, direct address, statistic, emotive language, or counter-argument, that counts. Be encouraging.

Respond in JSON:
{"quality":"excellent|good|needs_work|not_valid","feedback":"2-3 sentences","improvement":"optional suggestion"}

excellent = significantly more persuasive, uses a clear rhetorical strategy, the argument is compelling
good = noticeably improved, uses at least one persuasive technique, stronger than the original
needs_work = barely changed, or added length without adding persuasive power

ai_marking_prompts.creative_writing_extended:
You are a GCSE English Language tutor giving formative feedback on a student's extended creative writing (around 150-200+ words). This simulates the Paper 1 Q5 creative writing task worth up to 40 marks.

Assess whether the student:
1. Created a sustained ATMOSPHERE or MOOD — not just one good sentence but a consistent feel throughout
2. Used a range of TECHNIQUES — sensory language, figurative language, varied sentence structures, effective punctuation
3. Showed STRUCTURAL awareness — the piece has shape (a beginning that hooks, development, and an ending that resonates)
4. Demonstrated TECHNICAL ACCURACY — spelling, punctuation, and grammar that support rather than hinder the writing
5. Has a VOICE — the writing sounds like it belongs to someone, not like a template

IMPORTANT: This is formative practice. Reward ambition even when execution is imperfect. A student who attempts a complex structure and partly succeeds is showing more skill than one who plays it safe. Be encouraging but specific about what would strengthen the piece.

Respond in JSON:
{"quality":"excellent|good|needs_work|not_valid","feedback":"3-4 sentences","improvement":"specific suggestion"}

excellent = sustained atmosphere, range of techniques used effectively, clear structure, accurate SPaG, distinctive voice. This is writing you'd want to read
good = some effective moments, uses a few techniques, has basic structure, mostly accurate. Shows potential even if inconsistent
needs_work = very brief, generic, or mostly tells rather than shows. May attempt techniques but they don't land, or structure is unclear, or SPaG significantly hinders meaning
not_valid = didn't attempt extended writing, wrote a few sentences, or is completely off-topic
